Propositional Logic Formulation
For any given linguistic unit or string x, the sutra arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam (1.2.45) can be defined as a Boolean equivalence:


$$\text{Prātipadika}(x) \iff \text{Arthavat}(x) \land \neg \text{Dhātu}(x) \land \neg \text{Pratyaya}(x) \land \neg \text{Pratyayānta}(x)$$

Set Theory Formulation
If we treat the Sanskrit lexicon as a universe of strings U, the subset of nominal stems can be calculated through set difference:


$$P = A \setminus (D \cup R \cup E)$$

⚬ P = The set of all Prātipadika (nominal stems).
⚬ A = The set of all Arthavat (meaningful linguistic units).
⚬ D = The set of all Dhātu (verbal roots).
⚬ R = The set of all Pratyaya (affixes).
⚬ E = The set of all Pratyayānta (words ending in an affix).

Predicate Logic / Rule-Based Evaluation
To evaluate whether a given input string S receives the Prātipadika saṃjñā, the function requires a positive assertion of meaning followed by three negative constraints (exclusion filters) based on the text in 69742AC2-E844-475A-84E0-F02752B55512.png:


$$f(S) = \begin{cases} \text{True}, & \text{if } M(S) \text{ and } S \notin (\mathbb{D} \cup \mathbb{P} \cup \mathbb{P}_{anta}) \\ \text{False}, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

⚬ M(S): Asserts that S is arthavat (meaningful). Without this, individual meaningless phonemes (like 'dh', 'a', 'n' in 'dhan') would falsely trigger nominal operations.
⚬ \mathbb{D}: The catalog of verbal roots (adhātuḥ filter).
⚬ \mathbb{P}: The catalog of standalone affixes (apratyayaḥ filter).
⚬ \mathbb{P}_{anta}: The set of forms terminating in an affix, derived via the paribhāṣā maxim pratyayagrahaṇe tadantagrahaṇam (where stating a suffix inherently includes forms ending in that suffix).

history.text:
Propositional Logic Formulation
For any given linguistic unit or string x, the sutra arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam (1.2.45) can be defined as a Boolean equivalence:


$$\text{Prātipadika}(x) \iff \text{Arthavat}(x) \land \neg \text{Dhātu}(x) \land \neg \text{Pratyaya}(x) \land \neg \text{Pratyayānta}(x)$$

Set Theory Formulation
If we treat the Sanskrit lexicon as a universe of strings U, the subset of nominal stems can be calculated through set difference:


$$P = A \setminus (D \cup R \cup E)$$

⚬ P = The set of all Prātipadika (nominal stems).
⚬ A = The set of all Arthavat (meaningful linguistic units).
⚬ D = The set of all Dhātu (verbal roots).
⚬ R = The set of all Pratyaya (affixes).
⚬ E = The set of all Pratyayānta (words ending in an affix).

Predicate Logic / Rule-Based Evaluation
To evaluate whether a given input string S receives the Prātipadika saṃjñā, the function requires a positive assertion of meaning followed by three negative constraints (exclusion filters) based on the text in 69742AC2-E844-475A-84E0-F02752B55512.png:


$$f(S) = \begin{cases} \text{True}, & \text{if } M(S) \text{ and } S \notin (\mathbb{D} \cup \mathbb{P} \cup \mathbb{P}_{anta}) \\ \text{False}, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

⚬ M(S): Asserts that S is arthavat (meaningful). Without this, individual meaningless phonemes (like 'dh', 'a', 'n' in 'dhan') would falsely trigger nominal operations.
⚬ \mathbb{D}: The catalog of verbal roots (adhātuḥ filter).
⚬ \mathbb{P}: The catalog of standalone affixes (apratyayaḥ filter).
⚬ \mathbb{P}_{anta}: The set of forms terminating in an affix, derived via the paribhāṣā maxim pratyayagrahaṇe tadantagrahaṇam (where stating a suffix inherently includes forms ending in that suffix).
